year: c. 1970s (postmark: Granada[?], June — year digits unclear)
recipient: Mr. & Mrs. T. C. Barnes & Family, 5501 Gloucester, Austin, Texas, U.S. 78723
notes: Front: the Puerta de Alcalá at night, floodlit, with streaks of traffic light around it; the attic inscription reads "REGE CAROLO III ANNO MDCCLXXVIII" (in the reign of Charles III, 1778). Back: "326.— Madrid, Puerta de Alcala"; published by J. L. Gallegos, Madrid. A 15-peseta stamp honoring the architect Secundino Zuazo. The machine slogan cancel reminds senders that letters for Madrid and Barcelona must carry the postal district number. The circular postmark is only partly legible (it appears to read Granada), dated June, with an unclear year. Message: "Dearest Faye, Buddy & Family: You just can't imagine what a beautiful country Spain is and we're having a wonderful time. Donna is our guide. She speaks like a native and understands the customs of the country. She has reserved rooms in beautiful hotels for us in each town we plan to tour. The car we have engaged is a Renault. She handles it like a cowboy riding a bronk. People here drive like mad. I'm enjoying every minute — We don't get to bed before 2:00–3:00 A.M. Will have lots to tell you. Love Mom" A dealer sticker ("1843 $0.49") is on the address side; it matches the Jerusalem card and came from the same dealer lot.
feed_description: Mom writes home to Austin from Spain: Donna is their guide, speaks like a native and drives the rented Renault "like a cowboy riding a bronk," and nobody gets to bed before 2 or 3 A.M.

location: Aurora, Illinois — West Bridge across the Fox River
recipient: Mrs. Emma Loeper[?], Dacoma, Okla., Alfalfa Co.
notes: Front: "West Bridge across Fox River, Aurora, Ill." — a hand-tinted view of a triple-arched concrete bridge with a balustrade, a streetcar crossing, and a red-brick block on the far bank. Published by E. C. Kropp Co., Milwaukee, No. 6920. Back: divided "Post Card" back with a green 1-cent Washington stamp, postmarked Big Rock, Ill., Feb 22, 6 PM, 1913. Big Rock is a farm village about ten miles west of Aurora; "the Beacon" the writer promises to send is surely the Aurora Beacon newspaper. Dacoma is a small town in northwest Oklahoma; the card says "Alfalfa Co.," though Dacoma sits in Woods County just across the line. Feb 22, 1913 was a Saturday, so the "Thurs night" rain fits the dates. The message is written in pencil without punctuation; punctuation is not added here. The last lines turn into a joke: little Marion calls chicken pox "chicken box" and asks Ma to look for boxes on a chicken. Message: "Big Rock Feb 22th 1913 Dear Cousins received your card I sent you a letter and a card on the 13th and a card before that did you not receive them we had the worst sleet storm yesterday I ever saw it commenced to rain Thurs night at midnight rained all day yesterday and froze on the trees but last night it got warmer and at midnight the wind blew and some of the ice came off going north of town to Mells[?] there is 31 poles down and lots of wires down and the trees looks as though a cyclone had been along will send you the Beacon so you can read it Fannie's[?] children have the chicken pox Marion says the chicken box Ma see if there is any boxes on one snow squalls to day we got Vera's[?] picture Love to all[?] Sarah M" A dealer sticker ("1843 / 0.99") is on the address side, from the same dealer lot as the Madrid card.
feed_description: February 1913, Big Rock, Illinois: "the worst sleet storm I ever saw" — 31 telephone poles down, trees that look like a cyclone went through, and a child who calls it "chicken box."

recipient: Miss Iva Pirtle, R. 2, Fordland, Missouri
notes: Front: "Liberty Memorial, Kansas City, Missouri" — a real-photo view of the World War I memorial's tower between its two flanking halls, with the carved frieze on the north wall and the lawn and stairs below. Dedicated in 1926, the memorial is now home to the National WWI Museum and Memorial. Back: "This is a genuine Grogan photograph" (Grogan Photo Co., Danville, Illinois). A 1-cent green "For Defense" Statue of Liberty stamp (1940 National Defense issue), machine-cancelled Kansas City, Mo., Sep 19, 5 PM, 1944, with a "Post Card" slogan. Fordland is a small town in Webster County east of Springfield. Sept 19, 1944 was a Tuesday, matching the heading. Message: "Tues. 2-30 O'Clock Sept 19-44 Dear Iva: We got into K.C. about 10, & will leave out here to-night. Ruth & I went up & saw this memorial, in the picture it looks quite level, but really it is on quite a hill, it certainly a lovely place & view, you can see so far. It is World War I Memorial. It was raining here when we got here but has cleared off & the sun is really hot. Lots of Love Lora[?] & Ruth" A pencil dealer mark ("527.50") is on the address side, matching the Menlo Park convent card.
front: 1944 - Liberty Memorial, Kansas City, MO - front.jpeg
back: 1944 - Liberty Memorial, Kansas City, MO - back.jpeg
feed_description: Two travelers climb up to Kansas City's Liberty Memorial in September 1944: "in the picture it looks quite level, but really it is on quite a hill."

sender: Pvt. Sherman H. Osborn, 37112487[?], B. Co. of M.P.[?], Fort Riley, Kansas
recipient: Mrs.[?] Sherman Osborn, Box 383, Edmonds, Washington (the message is to "Aunt Addie")
notes: Front: "15805. Union Station, Denver, Colorado" — a linen-style tinted view of the station's granite and terra-cotta front with its three great arched windows, a row of 1930s cars parked out front. Published by the H. H. Tammen Co., Denver ("H-H-T-Co" arrow logo). The printed back text reads: "The Union Station is one of the most beautiful in this section of the country. The main waiting room is 100 feet by 110 feet. Seats 400 people comfortably. Waiting room 67 feet high. The cost of the main building alone was $500,000. Built of granite and terra cotta." Back: no stamp — "Free" is written in the stamp box, the free-mail privilege granted to servicemen during World War II. Machine-cancelled Junction City, Kans., Apr 4, 6:30 PM, 1944; Junction City is the town just outside Fort Riley. The soldier wrote his return address across the top; the serial number and unit abbreviation are hard to read and flagged. The address is in a different, neater hand from the message. Manhattan, Kansas (where he spent Saturday night) is about 20 miles east of Fort Riley. The message has almost no punctuation; light punctuation follows his own dots. Message: "Aunt Addie. just a line to say hello and tell you that I am just fine and hope the same with you. These[?] nice fine day. The weather is sure nice out here in Kansas. How is it out that way fine & hope. I hope this card finds you all well at home Thursday. I was[?] over at Manhattan last sat night & was it cold over there Aunt Addie. well so long for this time. Sherman H. Osborn" A pencil dealer mark ("1.00") is on the address side.
feed_description: A private at Fort Riley sends a free soldier's card to Aunt Addie in Washington state, April 1944: the Kansas weather is "sure nice," but Manhattan was cold last Saturday night.

recipient: John W. Tutt[?], 1205 N. Cascade, Colo. Springs, Colorado
notes: Front: "Hotel Warren, Garden City, Kansas" — a linen-style view of the brick hotel on a street corner, with a rooftop "Hotel Warren" sign, a vertical "Warren Hotel" sign, a "Coffee Shop" arrow, an "Air Conditioned" Coca-Cola sign and "Pearl Drugs" in the ground floor. Back: "Pub. by Pearl Drug Store, Garden City, Kansas" (the drugstore pictured inside the hotel), card number 1166. A green 1-cent Washington stamp, deliberately placed upside down, machine-cancelled Garden City, Kans., Jun 19, 1948. The message is written across the card, crossing the postmark, and the address is written upside down relative to the message. The "4th" is partly hidden under the postmark but reads clearly enough. Message: "Dear John — 6/18/48 We had a very hot trip down. It was about 103° at 2 o'clock. Everyone asks for you and misses you. Upon our arrival Kies[?] conducted us on a tour of the new power plant. They are building a 4th story on this hotel. How are the movies? Much love, Mother" A pencil dealer mark ("527.50") is on the address side, matching the Liberty Memorial and Menlo Park cards.
feed_description: Mother writes to John in Colorado Springs from Garden City, Kansas, June 1948: 103° on the drive down, a tour of the new power plant, and a new story going up on the hotel.

location: Ogallala, Nebraska — "Mama — Can Jimmy Stay for Lunch?"
recipient: Miss Elaine Kennedy, 4201 N St., Lincoln, Nebr.
notes: Front: a black-and-white cartoon by Wm. Standing of a grinning cow with a flower in her mouth and two calves, one asking "Mama — Can Jimmy Stay for Lunch?" Back: "From an original etching by Wm. Standing, noted Indian artist"; published by Western Stationery Co., Yachats, Oregon. William Standing (1904–1951) was an Assiniboine artist from the Fort Peck Reservation in Montana, known for humorous ranch and reservation drawings sold widely as postcards. A green 1-cent Washington stamp, machine-cancelled Ogallala, Nebr., Sep 26, 10 AM, 1949. Sep 26, 1949 was a Monday, so "Sun Night" was the 25th. Ogallala sits on U.S. 30 (the Lincoln Highway), lined in those years with tourist courts like the Mission Courts. Message: "Ogallala Nebr. Sun Night. Here we are at the Mission Courts have a cute cabin bath Radio & garage — will be home tomorrow noon. Hope your fine, we are tired." A pencil dealer mark ("9744 1—") is in the upper corner.
feed_description: A cow cartoon by Assiniboine artist William Standing, mailed from Ogallala in 1949: a cute cabin at the Mission Courts with bath, radio and garage — "will be home tomorrow noon."

recipient: Dr. & Mrs. F. Eby, 2612 San Pedro, Austin, Texas, U.S.A.
notes: Front: a color view from the mountainside above Kotor, looking across the town and its newer outskirts to the inner Bay of Kotor and the steep mountains beyond, with a switchback road climbing at right. The card is worn, with a torn lower-right corner. Back: "Kotor" and "Snimak: O. Hohnjec" (photo by O. Hohnjec); published by "Duvan" Kotor. The stamp has been torn away, leaving only the wavy cancel; the circular postmark reads Split 2, 10 VII, 13–14 h, with the year digits partly hidden. In 1961 Kotor and Split were both part of Yugoslavia. The recipient is very likely Frederick Eby (1874–1968), the longtime University of Texas professor of the history and philosophy of education, who lived in Austin. The writer's religious statistics are her own impressions. Message: "July 10 — Split. Kotor is a little harbor where we stopped en route to Dubrovnik where we stayed two nights. The scenery along the Dalmatian coast is a trifle like that of the Norwegian fjord country except that the vegetation is sub-tropical. The population of Dubrovnik is 100% R.C. so evidently the church flourishes in this land. In other parts some are Moslem, some Gk. Orthodox. We came here by boat yesterday. Tomorrow we go by train to Zagreb. Then back to Italy (Venice, Milan, Lake Como.) Love to all, Ruthe[?]" A dealer sticker ("1843 $0.39") is on the address side, from the same dealer lot as the Madrid card, also sent to Austin.
feed_description: A traveler writes to Austin from Split in July 1961: the Dalmatian coast is "a trifle like the Norwegian fjord country" but sub-tropical, and next it's the train to Zagreb.

recipient: Little Oleta Fo[?]... (surname runs off the edge), Utopia, Tex.
notes: Front: "Fishers Peak, Trinidad, Colo." — a tinted winter view of the flat-topped, snow-covered peak over bare cottonwoods and a frozen river. Fishers Peak (9,633 ft) rises just southeast of Trinidad and is now the centerpiece of Fishers Peak State Park (opened 2020). Back: "C. T. American Art" divided back (Curt Teich & Co., Chicago), stock number A-65750; the white-border style and Teich number suggest c. 1915–1925. No stamp and no postmark, so it was hand-delivered or sent in an envelope. The card is heavily worn and stained and written in faint pencil. The main message is to a small child, to keep and read when she is older. A second message runs up the left margin and through the "Post Card" lettering; only parts can be read. Utopia is a small town in the Texas Hill Country (Uvalde County). Message: "Grand Dear Little Oleta — Will send you a Post card to you Precious Little Darling. Nobody knows how bad I want to see all your precious little angels. You are too small now to know what I say. But possible you can keep and read it when your older and can understand. Be a sweet little girl[?] [last line worn away, illegible]" Side message (fragmentary): "[Th]is is a view of Fishers Peak which[?] [is 1]0,000 feet high just a few miles [from] town and directly in front[?] [of the house?] … [illegible] … of the … beautiful … out he[re] …" Pencil dealer marks ("#1843 $1.—") are on the address side, the same dealer lot as the Aurora, Kotor and Madrid cards.
feed_description: A faint pencil card from Trinidad, Colorado, to "Little Oleta" in Utopia, Texas — too small to read it yet, so "keep and read it when your older and can understand."
